QUIBBLE.name: Bill
QUIBBLE.direction: Old pompous pirate captain, gravelly theatrical boasts.

FINE PRINT.name: Charlie
FINE PRINT.direction: Quick, mischievous parrot, bright emphatic comic delivery.

NELL.name: Alice
NELL.direction: Clear, lively young adventurer; curious and dryly amused.

MARA.name: Matilda
MARA.direction: Warm, grounded tavern keeper; measured delivery and dry humour.

ORIN.name: Bill
ORIN.direction: Low, seasoned older navigator; unhurried storyteller.

records.text: If you came for a room, the roof only leaks on the expensive side.
You have the key. Consider it payment for services to tidiness.
An old chart. Bring back my brass tankard from the window table and you can have the key.
Look before you pick things up. Then pick them up anyway. That seems to be how adventurers work.
My tankard! Here, take the chest key. The chart inside deserves some fresh air.
I haven’t lost my ship. I know exactly which ocean it’s in.
That chart marks Bellweather Shoal. Bring a boat. I’ve tried walking.
Mara keeps a chart in that chest. She might part with the key if you help clear up.
I got lost professionally until someone started paying me.
A warm fire. A cold harbour. And absolutely no plan.
What’s in the sea chest?
Any advice for a new arrival?
Where should I start?
How did you become a navigator?
I’ll let you get back to it.
I'm looking for surveying work.
Then you've come to a place with water and disagreements.
I brought a pencil.
Good. Most applicants bring another disagreement.
Does anyone need a chartmaker?
Everyone needs an accurate chart. Paying for one remains a minority interest. There's an old survey in that chest.
What's in the sea chest?
Why don't you fetch the tankard?
Because I have six customers' washing-up and one customer's ambition to encourage.
Can I keep the chart?
A chart ought to go somewhere. That one has mostly been under a blanket.
The markers don't agree with it.
Then check which one has changed. Old doesn't always mean wrong.
Do you know who made it?
People who knew this harbour before it acquired an advertising budget.
One tankard acquired. My career in piracy begins modestly.
Locked. Perhaps Mara knows where the key is.
A chart to Bellweather Shoal! Finally, a plan with a suspicious dotted line.
These aren't decorative arrows. Someone measured the ebb channel.
But the new marker outside points across it. Either this chart has aged badly, or somebody's improved the water.
The key can stay on its hook. One less mystery in my pockets.
The tankard is already taken care of.
Wrong sort of tumbler.
Too heavy. I'd have to chart a route just to lift it.
A dramatic edit. I'll try a pencil first.
An inspired combination. Unfortunately, the universe disagrees.
Best leave that where it is.
It is keeping its thoughts to itself.
A fine brass tankard. Someone has engraved property of Mara underneath.
A sturdy sea chest. Its lock has survived more voyages than I have.
Shoreline observations wanted. Payment on verification. Below that: ship's cook wanted. Must distinguish salt from gunpowder.
A warehouse corner, a lighthouse, and some very new buoys. Out there: a thousand possible adventures. In here: better heating.
The only member of this establishment with a reliable work ethic.
Mara runs a tight ship. Particularly impressive for a building.
A navigator who has misplaced his ship. Promising.
Have you lost a ship?
I haven't lost my ship. I know exactly which ocean it's in.
Where did you last see it?
At the berth indicated by an entirely official marker. It was a very reassuring marker.
Can you read this chart?
Bellweather Shoal. And the old transit marks. Match those from the outer landing before you trust either set of buoys.
What is a transit mark?
Two fixed marks. Line them up and you know where you're looking. Much less opinionated than a sailor.
Which way should the water run?
Depends on the tide and the channel. Use the board at the landing. Don't mistake one swirl for a conspiracy.
Will you come with me?
Find out whether the bridge is admitting pedestrians today. I'll keep an eye on the water from here.
A work request headed Space Quest. One shelf. Six inches wider. Please. The bucket's been drawn as a rocket.
A space quest?
Six inches. The bucket's ambitious.
Mission accomplished. No worlds saved. Considerably less tripping.
That's how most useful jobs end.
Still six inches. Still a frontier.
Halt! Captain Quibble owns this bridge. Passage costs three bruises to my ego.
What are the rules?
Five exchanges. Win three and you cross. Nobody gets hurt. Take your time; I have a very small jurisdiction.
I don't have a sword.
There's a practice blade on that peg. Blunt as an unpaid compliment. We provide all necessary equipment.
This plaque says the bridge is public.
And the public has been very careless about defending it.
What does the company want?
Apparently my toll is an unauthorised obstruction. Their toll is infrastructure.
En garde... grammatically.
I'll let you get back to it.
A parrot with a ledger. Nature's warning against teaching birds arithmetic.
He has enough reputation for a fleet, and just enough bridge for himself.
One glorious victory. Exact change appreciated. Behind it: Fair Passage Company, harbour access agreements under review.
For the use of the harbour. I suppose the captain is technically using it.
A practice blade, thoughtfully blunted. Only pride gets hurt here.
Expenses: ink, crackers, ink-flavoured crackers. These accounts are private, unlike this allegedly public bridge.
You've won. I still insist on the last word.
Then make it welcome. You keep the word. I keep walking.
Welcome. Hm. That was almost civilised.
A temporary victory. The company's notice says it may replace all existing passage arrangements.
Including yours?
Especially mine. It uses the word all in a most aggressive manner.
The bridge is open to you. My dignity remains under repair.
An old survey, a new sign, and a harbour full of opinions. Time to make an observation.
The tide board says ebb. Its diagram shows the usual flow in this channel going left. The new company arrow points right.
Warehouse corner. Lighthouse notch. Fixed marks, unlike those floating buoys.
Stand here. Align warehouse corner with lighthouse notch. Finally, instructions that don't demand a subscription.
A current indicator, caught on that bolt. It tells me nothing while it's stuck.
Free of the bolt, still safely tethered. Now the water can speak for itself.
A public boathook. Return to rack. A refreshingly uncomplicated contract.
I can lift that snag with the boathook.
Pulling tightens the snag. I need to lift it with the boathook.
This works better when it stays in the water.
Paper is an excellent current indicator exactly once.
A brass company signal buoy. Too far to reach. Close enough to watch.
The monkey emblem of the Fair Passage Company. Their launch seems to know exactly where it's going.
I need the old chart from Mara's chest before I can make that comparison.
I should read the tide board first. A direction without a tide phase isn't much of an argument.
I should identify the fixed marks first. The warehouse corner and lighthouse notch look promising.
That's a floating marker. If it drifts, my whole argument drifts with it.
The buildings haven't moved. Reassuring, if you're a building.
This is the right channel. Now let's see whether the water agrees with the sign.
First I need to compare the chart at the sighting cleat.
The float is still snagged. I need a working indicator before I watch the channel.
Ebb tide. The float settles to the left, just as the board predicts.
Three amber flashes. Three bell strokes. That's a deliberate signal.
Now the float has swung right. Those leaves are going with it. The board still says ebb.
And the company launch enters immediately, following the new arrow.
A current can surprise a chart. That's why people like me get work.
But the bell knew first. And that boat was ready. Someone knows something the rest of the harbour doesn't.
I have observed one channel, not interviewed an ocean. Let's keep to what I actually saw.
The change was local and coordinated with company traffic. Find out who operates the signals and whether this has happened before.
If the harbour's doing tricks, somebody has already written a terrible headline.
Someone built that signal. Someone may remember how it's meant to work.
An official marker sent Orin to the wrong berth. I'd like to see which one.
I came looking for a job. I appear to have found a question. Tomorrow, I'll find out who else is asking it.
A company boat knew when the current would turn.
Then write down what you saw. People argue less successfully with a date and a drawing.
Then start with the signal, not with my reputation. One of those can still be repaired cheaply.
Of course. Their signs are larger. Are we investigating that, or something worse?
The company wants me to sign its agreement before asking that question.
I should finish this observation before chasing another lead.
I keep score. Conflict of interest? I prefer confluence of income.
A toll booth with swords. Finally, honest advertising.
A fine sentence. Shame it arrived without a point.
My ego is thoroughly perforated. The bridge is yours to cross.
Squawk! We lost the duel, but retained the merchandising rights!
Keep them. I only wanted the right of way.
Three dents in your composure. Come back with a sharper argument.
Right. Less swordplay, more wordplay. Let's try that again.
My fearsome reputation always precedes me!
Blast. Even my reputation has left me waiting.
Then I'll fight your reputation while you catch up.
Mine travels by carriage.
Your hat is smaller than advertised.
Squawk! Bridge toll: one gold coin per foot. Wings cost extra!
My bill? That's outrageous! It's already full of crackers!
I demand a receipt with feathers.
Put it on your bill. You've already got one.
What if I cross on my elbows?
I can tie an enemy in seventeen different knots!
I am a terror of the seas, not formal wear!
I can count to eighteen.
Your shoelaces disagree.
Wonderful. I've been looking for a bow tie with ambition.
Every word spoken on this bridge belongs to me. Pay the royalties!
Taxes? I resign! This bird is now a non-prophet organisation!
Then these unpaid taxes belong to you too.
I shall speak exclusively in soup.
Polly wants a lawyer.
Nobody crosses my bridge until I have the last word!
Welcome. Wait. That felt suspiciously like cooperation.
Last word! There, I've stolen it.
Say welcome. You get the last word; I get across.
I'll build a taller bridge.
A fine brass tankard. Someone has engraved “PROPERTY OF MARA” underneath.
WANTED: ship’s cook. Must distinguish salt from gunpowder. Previous cook need not apply.
Out there: a thousand possible adventures. In here: substantially better heating.
The harbour can wait. There is still a perfectly good mystery indoors.
Look at
Inside: a chart to Bellweather Shoal. Our next destination.
Too heavy. Perhaps I should try opening it.
It is already unlocked. Bellweather Shoal awaits.
The chart points to Bellweather Shoal. Our adventure starts here.
Beyond this door lies the next chapter. For now, this is our development room.
Select something from your pockets, then click what you want to use it with.
An image could not be loaded. Please reload the page.
Progress saved. Even adventurers deserve a safety net.
Saving is unavailable in this browser. Your current room is still playable.
No saved game yet.
Back where we left off. The tankards have missed you.
That save could not be loaded. Your current game has been kept.
A fresh start. Same suspiciously welcoming tavern.
Three clear evenly spaced brass buoy bell strokes over quiet open air. No speech, no music.
Small wooden harbour launch passes gently across calm water with a soft low engine putter and water ripples. No voices or music.
A wooden pole gently lifts a rope off a rusty bolt, a quiet creak followed by a small cork splashing into water. No voices or music.
Quiet small wooden footbridge over a seaside harbour at night, gentle water lapping against pilings, faint rigging tapping and sea breeze. No music, no speech, no loud events. Seamless loop.
Two light fencing swords meet with a crisp metallic clink and a brief swish. Playful theatrical practice duel. No voices or music.

Quiet interior of a small wooden seaside tavern at night. Gentle close fireplace crackle, distant soft harbour waves and occasional low timber creaks. Calm warm intimate atmosphere, no music, no speech, no loud events. Seamless background loop.

Steady unhurried footsteps of one person in soft leather boots walking on old wooden tavern floorboards. Quiet rhythmic hollow footfalls and subtle wood creaks, close dry recording, no voices or music. Seamless loop.
Single brass tankard lifted from a wooden table, short light metallic clink and faint scrape. Close dry game sound effect, no voices or music.
Brass tankard set gently on a wooden counter, followed by a small brass key jingling into a palm. Two delicate metallic clinks. Close dry game sound effect, no speech, no music.
A small brass key turns in an old lock with a satisfying click, then a wooden sea chest lid creaks open softly. Close dry game sound effect, no voices or music.
